title: Jeremiah 23:1–8
context: The LORD pronounces woe on the shepherds, Judah’s rulers, especially its kings after the oracles of chapter 22, who have scattered his flock (23:1–2). He promises to gather the remnant himself and set up faithful shepherds (23:3–4), to raise to David a righteous Branch called “The LORD our righteousness” (23:5–6), and to bring about a new exodus from the north (23:7–8). The Branch promise rests on the Davidic covenant of 2 Samuel 7 and is shared ground; readers in both traditions commonly hear it as fulfilled in Christ. Jeremiah 33:14–16 reuses the Branch promise, applying the name to the city, and 23:7–8 closely repeats 16:14–15; these are noted without harmonizing.

verses.text: “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD speaks: “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture!” Arminian readers see leaders held responsible for the harm they do, since the flock belongs to the LORD and not to them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD claiming the flock as his own and judging unfaithful rulers. In context the shepherds are Judah’s rulers, especially its kings, addressed in chapter 22, and readers in this tradition see leadership as a stewardship.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, says against the shepherds who feed my people: “You have scattered my flock, driven them away, and have not visited them. Behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “You have scattered my flock, driven them away, and have not visited them.” Arminian readers note the wordplay: the shepherds failed to visit the flock, so the LORD will visit their evil on them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the measure-for-measure judgment in the repeated word “visit.” Neglect of the people is treated as a real wrong, and the LORD himself takes up the cause of the scattered flock.

verses.text: “I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they will be fruitful and multiply.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them.” Arminian readers see the LORD’s mercy outlasting judgment, with the scattering ascribed to God and to the shepherds alike.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the LORD says “I have driven them” while also blaming the shepherds in 23:2. Readers in this tradition see God’s rule over the exile and his faithful purpose to regather a remnant.

verses.text: I will set up shepherds over them who will feed them. They will no longer be afraid or dismayed, neither will any be lacking,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will set up shepherds over them who will feed them.” Arminian readers see the promise of faithful leaders who will care for the people, so that fear and loss give way to security.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God providing good shepherds after the failure of bad ones. Many readers in this tradition connect the promise with the fuller shepherd themes of Ezekiel 34 and John 10, cited here by reference.

verses.text: “Behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that I will raise to David a righteous Branch; and he will reign as king and deal wisely, and will execute justice and righteousness in the land.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will raise to David a righteous Branch; and he will reign as king and deal wisely.” Arminian readers ground the promise in the Davidic covenant of 2 Samuel 7 and commonly hear its fulfillment in Christ.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise root the Branch in 2 Samuel 7 and read it as fulfilled in Christ, the Son of David. Readers in both traditions commonly hold this messianic reading while also recognizing the promise’s setting in Judah’s failing monarchy.

verses.text: In his days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell safely. This is his name by which he will be called: The LORD our righteousness.
verses.arminianNotes: “This is his name by which he will be called: The LORD our righteousness.” Arminian readers hear Christ as the righteousness of his people, the ground of their acceptance with God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear Christ as his people’s righteousness and often connect the name with justification by his righteousness. Jeremiah 33:16 reuses the name for the city, a difference noted here without harmonizing.

verses.text: “Therefore, behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that they will no more say, ‘As the LORD lives, who brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt;’
verses.arminianNotes: “… they will no more say, ‘As the LORD lives, who brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt.’” Arminian readers see a coming deliverance so great that it will eclipse the exodus in memory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a new exodus promised. These lines closely repeat Jeremiah 16:14–15 with small differences in wording, and readers in this tradition note the reuse without forcing the two into one form.

verses.text: but, ‘As the LORD lives, who brought up and who led the offspring of the house of Israel out of the north country, and from all the countries where I had driven them.’ Then they will dwell in their own land.”
verses.arminianNotes: “As the LORD lives, who brought up and who led the offspring of the house of Israel out of the north country.” Arminian readers see the return from exile as a fresh demonstration of God’s saving faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s covenant faithfulness in the promised return. Some readers in this tradition see the promise reaching beyond the return from Babylon to a fuller gathering under the Branch, while holding that application with care.
